prompt.context: Our client, Steel Corp, is a privately held automotive flat steel producer serving North American automotive OEMs. The steel industry as a whole has experienced steady growth over the last decade due to increased North American auto production. In the past, Chinese and Brazilian steel imports have taken a significant portion of North American market share, however recently the markets have seen a more stable distribution.
prompt.question: Steel Corp has asked us to develop a strategy that would allow them to reach 30% market share by 2025. (Currently 2015)

clarifying_info.q: What is Steel Corp current production and capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Current production: 4,000,000 tons per year. Current production capacity: 4,600,000 tons per year. Current market share: 20%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current state of the flat steel market?
clarifying_info.a: Current price of steel is $500 per ton and is expected to increase 20% over the next decade. Average margin per ton is 15%. Steel demand is expected to rise 25% over the next decade.

1) New Steel: 15% market share (privately held), Max Capacity 4,000,000 tons. 2) National Steel: 25% market share (publicly held), Max Capacity 6,500,000 tons. 3) HD Steel: 10% market share (privately held), Max Capacity 2,500,000 tons. 4) Imports: 30% market share. There are no production constraints for competitors.
OEMs typically maintain long-term relationships and will rarely switch suppliers. All OEMs are expected to grow at an equal rate, so market shares will remain constant in 2025.

clarifying_info.q: What are the barriers to building new production capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Capital projects within this industry usually have extremely long lead times, sometimes taking 10-15 years to get a new facility up and running. Governments can impose import restrictions.

framework: Market analysis: size the current and future market, understand demand growth, pricing trends, and import dynamics
Competition: map competitor market shares, capacity, and ownership structure to identify M&A targets
Customer analysis: understand OEM relationships, switching behavior, and growth projections
Capability and capacity: assess Steel Corp production vs. required production to reach 30% share
Growth options: evaluate organic growth (new facility, capacity utilization) vs. inorganic growth (acquisition) against the 2025 deadline
Recommendation: select the best path and quantify value

questions.prompt: Calculate the total market size in 2015 and 2025, then determine how many tons Steel Corp must produce in 2025 to hold 30% market share.
questions.guidance: A strong answer builds a production table for all players. Steel Corp produces 4M tons at 20% share, implying a 2015 total market of 20M tons. With 25% demand growth, the 2025 market is 25M tons. 30% of 25M = 7.5M tons required. Steel Corp current capacity is only 4.6M, creating a shortfall of 2.9M tons that cannot be filled organically in the timeframe.

math.setup: 2015 total market = Steel Corp production / Steel Corp market share = 4,000,000 / 0.20 = 20,000,000 tons. 2025 total market = 20,000,000 x 1.25 = 25,000,000 tons. Required production at 30% = 25,000,000 x 0.30 = 7,500,000 tons. Production shortfall = 7,500,000 - 4,600,000 (max capacity) = 2,900,000 tons.
steps: 2025 production needed at 30% share: 25,000,000 x 0.30 = 7,500,000 tons
Shortfall vs. current max capacity: 7,500,000 - 4,600,000 = 2,900,000 tons
math.answer: Steel Corp needs to produce 7.5M tons by 2025 and faces a 2.9M-ton capacity shortfall.

questions.prompt: What are Steel Corp strategic options to close the 2.9M-ton capacity gap by 2025, and which is most viable?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify: (1) Build a new facility - ruled out because lead times are 10-15 years, beyond the 2025 horizon; (2) Organic market-share gains - ruled out because OEMs rarely switch suppliers; (3) Acquire a competitor - most viable because it simultaneously adds production capacity and locks in existing OEM customer relationships. New Steel (15% share, 4M-ton max capacity, privately held) is the most appropriate target, as its capacity covers the 2.9M shortfall and it is privately held (easier to acquire than a public company).

math.setup: Optional valuation estimate: additional capacity needed = 2,900,000 tons. Margin per ton = 500 x 0.15 = 75. Annual incremental margin = 2,900,000 x 75 = 217,500,000.
steps: This provides a rough floor for acquisition value reasoning
math.answer: Roughly $217.5M in annual incremental margin justifies a significant acquisition premium for the capacity alone.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks associated with acquiring New Steel?

categories.name: Financial / Valuation
ideas: Acquisition price may not make economic sense given margin multiples
Difficulty financing a large private acquisition

categories.name: Regulatory / Antitrust
ideas: Combined entity (~35% share) may attract antitrust scrutiny
Government import restrictions could shift competitive dynamics

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Long lead times if new capacity needs to be brought online post-acquisition
Cultural fit and management integration challenges
Raw material sourcing and long-term supply obligations

categories.name: Customer
ideas: OEM customers of New Steel may have contractual protections or loyalty concerns

categories.name: Market
ideas: Import competition could intensify, compressing margins
Steel price volatility affects profitability assumptions

recommendation: Steel Corp should acquire New Steel, a privately held competitor with 15% market share and up to 4M tons of production capacity, to close the 2.9M-ton capacity gap and reach 30% market share by 2025
A secondary option is to take a controlling interest (51%) in publicly traded National Steel, which offers even greater capacity but comes with higher complexity and cost
risks: New facilities cannot be built in time (10-15 year lead times exceed the 2025 deadline)
Winning new OEM customers organically is near-impossible given long-term relationship dynamics
Antitrust review could block or delay the acquisition
Acquisition premium may be high relative to standalone margin value
next_steps: Commission detailed due diligence on New Steel financials, operational capacity, and OEM contracts
Engage investment bank to advise on acquisition structure and valuation
Assess antitrust exposure with legal counsel
Develop integration roadmap to realize capacity and cost synergies post-close
